evidence.label: A Limiting Satisfiability Threshold for Every Fixed Clause Size
Linear Variance of the Random 3-SAT Hitting Time
Variance of the Random k-SAT Hitting Time

headline: Random k-SAT has a single limiting satisfiability threshold for every k ≥ 3, and the 3-SAT one is computable.
scope: It covers random k-SAT with independent clauses on distinct variables, sampled with replacement. It does not find the value of any threshold.
plain: Add random three-variable rules to a list until no setting of the variables obeys them all. The papers show that this switch happens at one fixed ratio of rules to variables for every rule size from three up. They also bound how much the stopping point wobbles, and show the 3-SAT ratio can be computed to any accuracy. Gaia Carenini proved the fixed-ratio part first.
doesNot: This does not give the numerical value of the 3-SAT threshold.
origin: This result comes from an unreleased OpenAI model, published in the openai/math release on 6 October 2026.

scorecard.firstStepBy: Vašek Chvátal and Bruce Reed, the limiting-threshold conjecture
scorecard.significanceWhy: It settles existence for every k with an independent proof and adds variance and computability results.

explanation:
Take three yes/no switches, x1, x2 and x3. A clause is a rule such as: x1 is on, or x2 is off, or x3 is on. It fails for exactly one of the 8 settings of the three switches. A formula is a list of such clauses, and it is satisfiable if some setting obeys all of them[1].

Now build a formula at random. Take n switches. Each new clause picks three different switches at random and flips a fair coin for each sign. Keep adding clauses. Early on, a setting that obeys everything almost surely exists. Later, almost surely none does. This is random 3-SAT, and the same game with k switches per clause is random k-SAT.

A quick count shows where the change must happen by. One clause rules out a fixed setting with chance 1/8[13]. So after m clauses, the expected number of good settings is 2^n × (7/8)^m. With m = c × n clauses, this shrinks to zero once c is above log 2 / log(8/7), about 5.19. The number c is called the clause density.

For 3-SAT, earlier work showed the change happens between densities 3.52 and 4.4898[19]. Physicists predict it near 4.267[20]. In 1992, Chvátal and Reed conjectured that the change happens at one fixed density as n grows[2]. Friedgut proved in 1999, with an appendix by Bourgain, that the change is sharp, but around a density that might still drift with n[3]. That drift was the obstacle[9]. Ding, Sly and Sun settled the question for all large enough k[4].

The first paper proves that for every k ≥ 3 the change happens at a single limiting density[5]. Below it, formulas are satisfiable with probability tending to one. Above it, the probability tends to zero. It says nothing about the density exactly at the threshold[6]. Gaia Carenini resolved this conjecture first, in work made public on 5 October 2026. The paper credits her with priority and gives a different proof[7,8].

The proof has two halves. A switch is called forced when every good setting gives it the same value[10]. The paper bounds how many switches are forced along the way. That shows the stopping point barely wobbles around its average. But a steady average can still drift as n grows[11]. So the paper compares a large system with two independent smaller ones[12]. It shows the drift must die out.

A second paper studies that wobble directly. Add clauses one at a time and stop at the first unsatisfiable formula. For k ≥ 4, it proves that the variance of the stopping time grows like n[14]. Variance measures the typical squared distance from the average. For k = 3 it proves a bound of order n log n. A third paper, from 5 October 2026, claims to remove that log factor for k = 3[15]. Variance of order n means the typical wobble is a fixed multiple of √n. With 10,000 switches, √n is 100, against about 42,670 clauses at density 4.267.

A fourth paper proves that the 3-SAT threshold is computable[16]. One fixed program can output it to any accuracy you ask for[17]. The program checks certificates from below and from above until they are close enough[22]. It does not compute the actual value, or confirm the 4.267 prediction[21]. It also gives no bound on how long the program runs[18].

How sure is this? Lean, a computer proof checker, has formal versions of three results. They are the threshold for every k ≥ 3, and the variance bounds. They also cover computability of the 3-SAT threshold. For k = 3, Lean has the n log n upper bound, not the sharper bound of the October paper. No specialist review of these papers has been published.
hypeCheck: Major if the proofs hold, but Carenini has priority for existence. Lean has formal versions of the threshold, variance and computability results; the linear 3-SAT variance is not in it.

glossary.meaning: A rule saying at least one of a few switches has a stated value.
Some setting of all the switches obeys every clause.
The number of clauses divided by the number of switches.
The density where satisfiable formulas turn from almost certain to almost impossible.
A switch that has the same value in every setting that obeys the formula.
The average squared distance of a random number from its own average.
A number that one fixed program can output to any requested accuracy.
